entries.def: [Two actions that need similar periods of time.]
entries.example: Pat got ready while I cooked the dinner.
entries.group: Two things happening at the same time

entries.def: [A longer action 'on my way to work' and a shorter action 'the accident'. We can also use when or as here.]
entries.example: The accident happened while I was on my way to work.
entries.group: Two things happening at the same time

entries.def: [For two short actions happening at the same time we use as, and we can add just for emphasis, e.g. He opened the door just as I rang the bell.]
entries.example: I saw him (just) as I came out of the office.
entries.group: Two things happening at the same time

entries.example: We met the others in the café, and then/afterwards we went to the match.
I finished my homework, and after that/afterwards I played some computer games.

entries.def: We can use afterwards instead of 'after that', and especially if one thing happens soon after another
entries.example: e.g. We had a couple of drinks, then afterwards we went back to the flat.

entries.def: If something happens after a lot of time or problems, you can use eventually or in the end, in place of finally
entries.example: e.g. The weather was bad and the traffic was awful, but eventually we got there.

entries.def: If something happens after a lot of time or problems, you can use eventually or in the end, in place of finally

entries.example: Well, for one thing it's too big to go in the space.
And for another, it's very noisy.

entries.def: For a second or final reason, we also use anyway in spoken English.
entries.example: We can't go to that club because it's too far. Anyway, I'm not a member.
